PrEP in SA

By: James Carroll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa has become the second country in the world to allow widespread access to groundbreaking HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis medication

Summary:
The Medicines Control Council of South Africa has have allowed a new, extremely easy to use and powerful weapon to stop HIV-negative South Africans from ever contracting the virus. The MCC has officially registered the use of a combination pill of two anti-retroviral drugs as a form of pre-exposure prophylaxis (or “PrEP”) medication; a pill taken once a day that massively reduces the chances of contracting the HIV. With South Africa’s high HIV burden, the deployment of this new intervention is profound. As of today, any general medical practitioner can prescribe PrEP. South Africans with private medical aid can motivate for PrEP to be covered by their medical plan. This vital new development in the fight against Aids it is now more crucial than ever that remaining barriers to accessing PrEP are removed. Fundamentally this means educating South Africans that PrEP exists and may help them personally and making sure that PrEP can be feasibly delivered in public healthcare settings. South Africa’s Anova Health Institute, in collaboration with the Desmond Tutu HIV Foundation, is currently implementing the largest state sector housed demonstration project for the use of PrEP. This project, taking place in Cape Town and Johannesburg, will gain the vital experience necessary to enable the department of health to take PrEP to scale. The rollout of PrEP on a national level could be viewed as the single biggest push towards combating HIV infection in Southern Africa. The drug however is not without it's detractors however with some calling it a "party drug" and a permission slip for rampant sexual behaviour.

Press Release:


PrEP4HIV
Could a ground-breaking new rollout of PrEP or a so-called pre-exposure prophylaxis drug, be the single biggest push yet towards combating HIV infection? Carte Blanche reports on the dramatic findings of a new clinical trial showing that HIV-negative South Africans, taking only one pill a day, are protected from contracting the virus. Is this a turning point in the fight against Aids?


Script:


CLAIRE V.O

William Kekae lives just outside Zakariyya Park south of Johanesburg and works as a driver. He has been married to his wife Patricia for more than two years. The couple are looking forward to starting a family. There is however a problem – William is HIV positive.

Millions of people in our country face the same problem but we have recently reached a turning point in the fight against HIV.

CLAIRE O.S
South Africa has become one of the first African countries to license a fixed-dose combination of anti-retrovirals to be used as an oral pre-exposure prophylaxis.

CLAIRE V.O

Commonly known as PrEP, it is a way for people who don’t have HIV to prevent HIV infection by taking a pill every day.

In November 2015 the Medicines Control Council approved the use of Truvada and its generics - drugs already used in combination with other antiretroviral medications. Instead of being given to people who are who have diagnosed as positive to curb the disease, it offers a remarkable amount of protection to those who are still negative.

GRAPHIC
CLAIRE VO:
The regime works like this. After digesting the pill, the medication builds up in your t-cells which are an essential part of the immune system. After between a week and a month your t-cells are saturated. When you’re exposed to HIV, the virus tries to attack your cells in order to replicate but because the t-cells are protected, the HI virus dies off.

LINDA-GAIL BEKKER:
This is very exciting, I refer to it as the prevention revolution because we’re talking about things we haven’t talked about before in thirty odd years.

CLAIRE VO:
Professor Linda-Gail Bekker is the Deputy Director of the Desmond tutu HIV Centre in Cape Town.

LINDA-GAIL BEKKER:
I think the most exciting component of all of this is the randomized controlled studies that show a pill a day works. Ever single demonstration project thereafter across the world has shown it only gets better. Once people know that they’re taking an intervention that works, that they know what the intervention is and they know it can work for them as individuals, they do it.

WILLIAM KEKAE:
I feel like we have been given another change. Like those people who are infected with HIV can live a normal life as long as you take care of yourself.

CLAIRE VO:
William currently has an undetectable level of HIV thanks to strict adherence of his medicine. The combination of this and PrEP for Patricia allows them the freedom to conceive naturally rather than expensive invitro-fertilisation techniques that are beyond their means.

CLAIRE VO:

To test the effectiveness of PrEP researchers at San Francisco’s Kaiser Permanente Medical Center reported on the real-world experience of 657 people who started Prep between 2012 and 2015. Over 99% were men who have sex with men, 84% reported multiple sexual partners and 30% had HIV positive partners. The result? Exactly zero patients contracted HIV infection.

A similar demonstration is currently underway locally to show the effectiveness of PrEP within state sector clinics. This is to develop tools that will allow PrEP to be nurse-driven and scaled up by the Department of Health.

CLAIRE VO:
Penelope Daki, affectionately known as Sister Mimi, is a nursing sister working at the Health 4 Men clinic in Woodstock, Cape Town who is part of the nurse-driven demonstration.

PENELOPE DAKI:
Before I used to work with people who are already infected with HIV. I used to work in an ART situation, where people were anxious because you would meet discordant couples and stuff like that and people would be anxious. People are more confident now and they’re more hopeful of their future because of the existence of PrEP.

CLAIRE VO:
32 year old business man Kaylin Mendes is one of 150 gay men who are taking part in the prep demonstration in Cape Town. It’s limited to this group because the community is more likely to comply completely to the study requirements.

CLAIRE:
Does Prep not encourage risky behaviour?

KAYLIN:
When women started going on the contraceptive, the immediate thought was well you must be promiscuous if you are going on a contraceptive. But, it’s just somebody taking an added precaution to take more control over their life; it doesn’t mean the person is promiscuous.

CLAIRE:
While the current demonstration is focussed on men who have sex with men, the end goal is to use the data to help those who need it the most - young women.

JAMES MCINTYRE:
In young girls, that the rate of new infections is between 5 and 10%. In some areas of KwaZulu-Natal 10% of girls will be infected each year; terrifying numbers.

CLAIRE V.O
The facts are not new – the harsh reality is that South Africa has the world’s highest HIV infection count with 6.2 million people living with the virus. A lifeline then that one pill could potentially prevent as many as 340,000 new people per year from becoming infected.

CLAIRE V.O
Professor James Mcintyre is the CEO of Anova Health Institute – a non-profit organization that does research and technical assistance in South Africa mainly on HIV and related issues.

CLAIRE:
IS it okay that we're develop

PROF. JAMES MCINTYRE
PrEP, I think, is a really exciting new development in HIV prevention. So, somebody will take a pill a day and it is very effective in helping reduce the risk of them becoming HIV positive.

CLAIRE OS:
Should we be focusing on medication for HIV negative people or people who are already HIV positive who might need their own drugs and medication?

PROF. JAMES MCINTYRE
We have to do both. We have to treat, clearly, in this country we have to treat even more people. We have 3.2 million people already on anti-retroviral treatment and with new guidelines from the WHO we probably have to add another couple of million. We cant carry on allowing new infections to happen and then think we are going to treat our way out of the epidemic at the end. We know that if people are positive and are on anti-retroviral treatment their risk of transmitting the virus is almost zero. So we can stop new infections by treating people and we can stop additional new infections by giving people PrEP.

CLAIRE VO:
Gesine (Ge-see-na) Meyer-Rath is a doctor and infectious disease modeler with eleven years experience in economic evaluations of health care interventions.

CLAIRE VO:
Henry Mkwananzi, the senior manager at Fedhealth’s HIV/AIDS disease management program explained that members are considered on a case by case basis but it was in their best interest to provide prevention to sero-discordant couples.

CLAIRE VO:
The Department of Health subscribes to the latest recommendations set out by the World Health Organisation around pre-exposure prophalaxis and will be continuing to review and implement Prep and ARV treatment to those at high risk.
